https://www.ibtimes.co.uk/polish-opposit.text: More Poles are opposing Ukraine's accession to the European Union (EU) than ever before, reopening wounds rooted in World War II. Only 50% of Polish citizens support Ukraine's admission to the 27-member organisation, according to a survey conducted by the publicly funded Centrum Badania Opinii Społecznej (Public Opinion Research Center).The figure marks a dramatic fall from the 90% approval recorded in 2022, shortly after Russia invaded Ukraine on 24 February. Ukraine applied to become a member of the EU just four days later, citing extenuating circumstances. However, the EU has maintained that there is no shortcut to membership.Why the Polish Oppose Ukraine's EU AccessionOf those in favour of Ukraine's membership, only 9% said Ukraine should be admitted as soon as possible. Around 41% said the process should proceed at a normal pace. Of those surveyed, 40% are against Ukraine's accession, 23 percentage points higher compared with a similar poll in October 2023.The highest opposition came from Poles with right-wing beliefs (53%) and young adults, aged between 18 and 24 (58%). Moreover, 55% of the Polish public believe Kyiv may have to concede some territories to end the war. The most divisive question is related to foreign aid, where 39% said military, financial and humanitarian support are warranted while 27% said these were excessive.The loss of support from the Poles may be due to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's move of honouring the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) by signing a decree on 26 May 2026 that the nation's elite forces be referred to as 'Heroes of the UPA.' The UPA is highly regarded as heroes in Ukraine, having fought against Nazi Germany and paving the way for the nation's independence.In Poland, however, the UPA is remembered for atrocities committed between 1943 to 1945. This includes the Volhynia Massacres, which claimed around 100,000 Polish lives from July to August 1943. Victims were largely woman and children, though other casualties included Armenians, Czechs, Georgians, Russians, Jews, and even Ukrainians who were part of Polish families.Fraught Poland-Ukraine RelationsMuch has been done between World War II and 2026 to heal relations between the two countries. In 2024, Zelenskyy and Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk signed the Agreement on Security Cooperation between the two countries. Ukraine recognised that Poland has provided Kyiv with military support since the Russian invasion.However, Zelenskyy honouring UPA reopened World War II wounds. Poland stripped Zelenskyy of the Order of the White Eagle honour, the highest state recognition. Polish President Karol Nawrocki called Ukraine and Zelenskyy's move 'outrageous,' 'incomprehensible' and 'deeply disappointing.'European Parliament's WarningThe European Parliament, the EU's law-making body, criticised Zelenskyy's actions early this month, citing 'the disregard for Polish sensitivities and grief linked to the UPA's estimated tens of thousands of victims and their families. '(It is) a very strong signal, it's a warning to Ukrainian authorities not to create bad emotions and not to act against European values,' said Andrzej Halicki, a Polish member of the European Parliament.This could slow down Ukraine's acceptance into the EU, which has reportedly already been blocked by Hungary. According to reports, Hungary has asked for the postponement of the second and third negotiating clusters, which could have addressed Ukraine's integration into the EU single market as well as economic and social policies.

Photograph: Matt Hartman/AP View image in fullscreen The Vandenberg space force base near Santa Barbara, California. Photograph: Matt Hartman/AP California Reporters and military duo held at gunpoint by security at US space force base Officers reportedly believed invitees were trying to make unauthorized entry on to Vandenberg base in California Associated Press Wed 19 Aug 2026 20.41 EDT Last modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 20.44 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Five news reporters and two members of the military who were invited to an event at Vandenberg space force base in California were briefly detained at gunpoint by security officers who thought they were gatecrashers, according to local news reports. The incident happened Monday ahead of an invitation-only groundbreaking for a new training facility for missile operators at the federal airfield near Santa Barbara, California. Reporters from Noozhawk and KEYT were among those detained, and both outlets published articles detailing the detainment. In a statement to Noozhawk, a Space Launch Delta 30 public affairs spokesperson called the incident a breakdown in communication. “Vandenberg space force base is experiencing an increased number of unauthorized entry attempts,” the statement said. “Every potential unauthorized presence must be treated as a legitimate threat until proven otherwise. While we recognize this may have been unsettling, the security of the base and its personnel is our priority.” The reporters and military members were part of a convoy being escorted on to the base by uniformed public affairs staff in a government minivan when they were suddenly ordered out of their vehicles with their hands up, according to news reports. Officers pointed guns, sirens were sounded, and barricades went up at the gate entrance, KEYT reported. The two military members assigned to the base – one enlisted and one a junior officer – were handcuffed and placed in base vehicles, while the civilians were ordered to sit on a curb, Noozhawk reported. The reporters for outlets also including KSBY-TV and the Santa Maria Times/Lompoc Record were held for more than 30 minutes, causing them to miss the event. All were let go without further incident. “We respect the military’s need to provide security for the base,” Tom Bolton, Noozhawk’s editor in chief, said in a statement Wednesday. “But clearly what occurred was unfortunate and unnecessary, and potentially dangerous, as firearms were drawn.” Bolton said he hopes to have a conversation with base leadership later this week to review what happened in the hopes of preventing a similar occurrence in the future. https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/28/seou.text: South Korea's President’s Lee Jae Myung’s office demanded an apology from Ukraine for denying an agreement to keep the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war from its territory to Seoul confidential.The row was ignited by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's disclosure last week that his country had sent two North Korean soldiers to the South, adding that they were "not easy to capture alive".The intensifying dispute risks complicating Kyiv's efforts to obtain weapons from allies, including South Korea, to fight off bombardments from Russia.Hours after Zelenskyy's disclosure, South Korea's President Lee Jae Myung criticised the action."I do not know why the Ukrainian side broke the agreement and made the matter public, but it is very disappointing," he wrote on X.Zelenskyy's aide Dmytro Lytvyn sought to play down the disclosure, saying that the president had only made public the fact that the soldiers were handed to South Korea. Ukraine is an "open country", noted Lytvyn, saying that it would be “unusual” to hand over the soldiers in secret.But Seoul condemned it as a breach of trust.Seong Ghi-hong, senior presidential secretary for public relations, said in a statement late on Sunday that South Korea was "considering additional measures that may be necessary regarding this matter"."It is in itself a very serious matter that the Ukrainian side violated the confidentiality agreement between the two countries and made the disclosure unilaterally,” he said."But the Ukrainian presidential press office's false statement that there had been no confidentiality agreement, seriously undermines trust between the two governments and gravely damages friendly relations between the two countries," he added.The South Korean Presidential office demands "an official explanation and apology," said Seong.Ukraine captured early last year two North Korean soldiers among Pyongyang's troops fighting for Moscow. One of them said he served in a reconnaissance unit and while some North Korean soldiers had been trained to use Russian military equipment, he had not.The soldier said he was conscripted to the military aged 17 and had been serving since then. A South Korean lawmaker had previously said the pair wanted to live a "normal life" in the South of the Peninsula.Analysts believe Lee Jae Myung’s angry reaction to the confidentiality agreement risks sparking intense feuds with the nuclear-armed north, which could translate into further hostility towards Seoul."North Korea has been using the deployed soldiers to create a heroic narrative for regime propaganda, and the South Korean government appears concerned that confirming the prisoners' return to the South and publicising it could further fuel hostility towards Seoul," said Park Won-gon, a professor at Ewha Womans University.Beyond the ramifications within South Korea, the row also risks complicating Kyiv's requests to the ally for armaments supplies.South Korea has so far not provided lethal weapons to Ukraine, citing a domestic ban on militarily aiding countries at war. Nevertheless, it had been considering requests for defensive weapons, especially since North Korea deployed troops to support Russia.

There have been calls to remove clips of the real 2022 Seoul crowd crush from the game. Photograph: Vuk Valcic/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock View image in fullscreen People queue for a pop-up ‘Korean alley’ experience in Shoreditch, London, earlier this month before the release of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4. There have been calls to remove clips of the real 2022 Seoul crowd crush from the game. Photograph: Vuk Valcic/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock South Korea Outcry after Call of Duty maker uses real footage of deadly Seoul crowd crush in new video game Bereaved families have urged the publisher of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 to remove a clip from the game that shows a figure performing CPR and bodies lying in the street Raphael Rashid in Seoul Thu 29 Oct 2026 00.41 EDT Last modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 06.37 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Bereaved families in South Korea have demanded that the makers of Call of Duty remove harrowing footage of the deadly 2022 Seoul crowd crush from the latest instalment of the video game. The clips , which are seconds-long, appear in the opening moments of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 , and are used to represent a scenario of civilian casualties during a fictional North Korean invasion. One shows a scene of chaos with a figure performing CPR on a victim lying in the street. Another shows rows of bodies laid out in the road, and a victim being carried away on a stretcher. A total of 158 people were killed in a narrow alley in Seoul’s Itaewon nightlife district during the Halloween weekend in 2022. Two more have since been recognised as victims, having died from trauma caused by the disaster. “We are appalled that the chaotic and desperate scenes, in which countless citizens performed CPR to save one another and victims lay on the cold street, were used exactly as they were to create a scene in a game,” the bereaved families’ council and a coalition of civic groups said in a joint statement on Wednesday, demanding that the footage be removed. ‘The audience gets to be in on it’: How narrative-led gameplay is Call of Duty’s greatest weapon Read more They said people who had taken part in the rescue or witnessed the crush were still living with trauma, while hateful comments about the victims were spreading online in connection with the game’s premise. View image in fullscreen A screengrab from the Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 game released by Activision, which is made up of real news broadcast footage from Getty showing paramedics performing CPR during the 2022 Itaewon crowd crush. Composite: Youtube/Activision Activision, the game’s publisher, told the Yonhap news agency that “some actual news footage included in the game’s opening cinematic was utilised as an element to convey the fictional story within the work.” They added, “We had absolutely no intention of mentioning or treating lightly any actual tragic events, including the Itaewon tragedy.” The Guardian has contacted Activision for comment. The demand comes as the country marks the fourth anniversary of the crush on Thursday . Players in South Korea identified the clip after the game’s release, and Korean broadcasters have compared it side by side with footage filmed on the night of the crowd crush . The Korean Game Users Association called for an apology and for the footage to be replaced. Modern Warfare 4 follows a South Korean marine private fighting a North Korean invasion through recognisable Korean streets. The title had already become a political talking point before its release, with conservative politicians urging president Lee Jae Myung – who is pursuing a more conciliatory approach towards North Korea – to play the game to understand what they described as the threat from Pyongyang. It topped South Korea’s sales chart on Steam, the leading PC gaming platform, within days of its release. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmde.text: Image source, Thomas Traasdahl / Ritzau Scanpix / AFP via Getty Images By Wedaeli Chibelushi Published 1 hour ago Denmark has accused Russian intelligence services of plotting to assassinate a Ukrainian-American near Copenhagen, saying they had "planned" and "initiated" the attempt. Denmark's security and intelligence agency said it had stopped individuals who were intending to kill the person, named by Danish media as rapper Kyivstoner, at a concert in September. Two people were charged with attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service, and pleaded not guilty. Denmark's foreign minister said Russia's defence attachÃ© will now be expelled. Russia's Embassy in Denmark called the allegations "unsubstantiated" and said Copenhagen failed to provide evidence of Moscow's involvement. In a statement posted on social media, the embassy claimed a "Danish model" had emerged, which it described as a "Russian trace" allegedly being discovered and "exploited for a propaganda spectacle". It accused Denmark of "provocations" intending to "frighten the Danish population in order to justify... a prolonged confrontation with Russia". Russian state media cites the foreign ministry in Moscow as saying it will respond to the expulsion of its official "accordingly". Danish media named the target of the assassination attempt as the rapper known as Kyivstoner, whose real name is Albert Vasiliev. Denmark's security and intelligence agency (PET) said the individuals who allegedly tried to assassinate him were associated with a banned Danish gang named Loyal to Familia. The group is "known for extensive, serious and violent criminal activity", according to the agency. PET, which worked with police on the case, said three individuals were stopped while travelling by car near the music venue where Kyivstoner was set to perform on 25 September. Firearms and knives were found in the vehicle, PET said. Since then, two people linked to the case have been charged with attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service. Both individuals pleaded not guilty to the charges, local media reported. In July, Russia's FSB security service accused Vasiliev and the Ukrainian authorities of organising a "terrorist attack" on military facilities and personnel in Russia. The rapper denied this allegation on social media. In a statement on Friday, Danish Foreign Minister Lars LÃ¸kke Rasmussen said the alleged assassination attempt was Russian "intimidation" and an attempt to make Denmark "waver" in its support for Ukraine. Russia's defence attachÃ© must leave the country within seven days, Rasmussen said. He also said Denmark wants the EU to restrict the ability of Russians to travel throughout Europe, saying even though Denmark is already very reluctant to issue visas, Russians can still get a Schenegen visa in another country and travel to Denmark. Denmark wants these visas to apply only in the country that has issued them, he added.
